explanations.positive_explanation: This feature flags the standard boilerplate of an Apache License 2.0 header—i.e. the copyright line plus “Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0” through the “AS IS”/“WITHOUT WARRANTIES” disclaimer in code comments.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on section‐heading or title text (e.g. article headlines, menu labels, archive or section headers) rather than on ordinary running sentences.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects discourse-signposting cues—words that introduce emphasis, summaries or lists (e.g. “whatever,” “what,” “things,” “advantages,” “benefits,” “relevance”)—marking that a key point or enumerated item is about to follow.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron picks out top‐level document headers and metadata banners—things like legal case captions, file-license comment blocks, section titles and their decorative separators—i.e. the formal header text that marks the start of a document or major section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature lights up on discourse-level connectives and subordinators—words like “that,” “but,” “if,” “when,” “and,” “later,” “in fact,” “say,” “which,” etc.—that introduce new clauses, contrasts, explanations or temporal shifts in a sentence.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “header/boilerplate” detector—it lights up on the markers and tokens that introduce a document or section (titles, bolded lead‐ins, copyright/license headers, datelines, patent-claim boilerplate, article or blog headings, code-comment slashes, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron lights up on list-introducing tokens and constructions—words like “include,” “including,” or “in” when they herald an enumeration of items.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature is a boundary detector for top‐level code or markup declarations, firing on the punctuation tokens that terminate file headers, include/import directives, or start‐tags (e.g. the final “.” in a copyright/license line, the “.” before “.h,” the “>” closing an XML tag, or the newline ending an import or class declaration).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires whenever a token is being used as the opening word of a new heading/section or list‐item—that is, it flags tokens that start titles, paragraphs or discrete content blocks.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “dash‐marker” detector: it lights up on hyphens and dash-like punctuation used as separators or in compound names (license identifiers, comment bars, file-meta tags, chemical or program names, double-dashes in text, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the highly structured “front‐matter” of judicial opinions and similar legal documents – the block of tokens that lays out the court name, docket or slip-op number, case caption (parties), decision date, publication and reporter references, etc. It’s essentially detecting the standardized header metadata format used in court opinions.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires whenever a token is a word-final fragment (a common subword “suffix”) – in other words, it marks the last piece of a word.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects the “names of” phrase in BSD‐style license disclaimers—specifically the clause forbidding use of the names of copyright holders or contributors to endorse or promote.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects the double-asterisk “**” markers used to bold or emphasize section headings and labels (e.g. “**News**,” “**Main menu**,” “**Oct. 16,…**”), thereby signaling the start of a new content block or header in formatted text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects opening‐curly‐brace tokens (“{” or “{{”) that introduce a new block, object literal, or interpolation across different languages and templating syntaxes.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires at the end of standalone header or metadata lines—titles, section headings, dates, labels—marking the boundary between a document’s “headline” line and the start of its body text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron detects document-level “front-matter” or structural metadata tokens—e.g. section and subsection headers, legal case captions and docket numbers, import/module or XML prolog lines, crystallography formulas, etc.—the standardized title/heading syntax that bookends or organizes a document.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron responds to “headline‐style” front‐matter in news/blog text—i.e. the titles, section headings, bylines or disclaimer lines (episode markers, date lines, newsletter/legal notices) that sit atop an article. It flags those meta-text chunks that look like headlines or top-of-page labels.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the final “.” that terminates a standalone heading or title-style sentence—i.e. the period ending the initial summary line of a document or section (patents, paper titles, blog headings, product intros, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “Celtic‐name prefix” detector – it fires on the character or bigram immediately following a Mc- or O′- prefix in surnames (e.g. McGuinness, McAuliffe, O’Reilly), marking those as proper‐name subwords.
